readerTitle: Same sales, opposite plans: small business or startup?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (나무 상자·팔레트 제조사, 배송 경로 앱, 물리치료 클리닉 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 정의는 Paul Graham, Steve Blank의 글에서 인용
insight: 스몰 비즈니스와 스타트업을 가르는 것은 크기나 업종, 기술이 아니라 '처음부터 무엇을 하도록 설계했는가', 즉 성장 경로와 자금 구조다. 같은 숫자도 어느 경로냐에 따라 건강 신호가 되기도, 위기 신호가 되기도 한다.
misconception: 스타트업은 기술 회사이고 스몰 비즈니스는 작은 가게다. 적자는 무조건 나쁜 신호이고, 연 10% 성장은 무조건 좋은 신호다.

sources.text: Blank, S. & Dorf, B. (2012). The Startup Owner's Manual (스타트업 정의: 반복 가능하고 확장 가능한 비즈니스 모델을 찾는 임시 조직)
모든 사업 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Paul Graham 인용 "A startup is a company designed to grow fast."는 2012년 에세이 'Startup = Growth'의 첫 문장입니다. 게시 전 원문 문구를 다시 확인하세요.
Steve Blank의 정의("a temporary organization designed to search for a repeatable and scalable business model")는 블로그와 저서에 여러 형태로 나옵니다. 카드에는 직접 인용 대신 풀어 쓴 표현을 썼습니다. 표현이 원뜻과 맞는지 확인하세요.
벤처 투자자는 대부분의 투자가 실패하고 소수가 큰 수익을 내는 구조를 전제한다는 내용은 일반적인 설명으로만 썼고 구체적 비율은 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Same sales. One made $150k, one lost $400k. Both owners are happy.
body: A crate and pallet maker sold $1 million last year and kept $150,000 in profit. A delivery-routing app also sold $1 million and lost $400,000.
Neither owner is worried. That isn't a mistake. They built two different kinds of business, and the same numbers mean opposite things in each.

image.label: A wooden pallet and a phone with a route map, side by side on a scale
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저울 양쪽에 나무 팔레트 더미와 배송 경로 지도가 뜬 스마트폰. 저울은 수평. 팔레트 위에 "+$150k", 스마트폰 위에 "−$400k" 꼬리표. 실제 로고나 앱 화면은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: An investor wants your crate business to go national.
body: You run the crate and pallet maker: $1M in sales, $150k profit, growing about 10% a year from regular local customers.
An investor offers $2M for a quarter of the company. The plan: open plants in new regions, accept losses for three years, aim for ten times the sales. What do you do first?

options.text: Take it. Growth capital like this rarely comes twice
options.feedback: You gain cash and ambition but give up profit, a quarter of the company and the right to grow slowly. If the market can't support ten times the sales, you're left with losses and a partner who expected more.

options.text: Decline. A profitable business shouldn't take risks
options.feedback: This may well be the right answer, and it keeps you in control. But you'd be deciding by habit, without checking whether a much bigger business is actually possible.

options.text: First check whether crates can really grow tenfold: demand, shipping costs, competitors in each region
options.feedback: Crates are heavy and bulky, so they're usually made close to customers. The question isn't whether growth is good. It's whether this business can grow that fast at all.

cards.title: Five years, two paths.

breakdown.label: Routing app, doubling yearly
breakdown.detail: $1M × 2⁵. Losses paid by investors along the way

breakdown.label: Routing app, +10% a year
breakdown.detail: Same growth as the crate maker, but still losing money. A failure

cards.callout: 10% growth is healthy for the crate maker and a crisis for the app. A $400k loss is the plan for the app and a crisis for the crate maker.

cards.title: Small business vs startup
body: A **small business** is built to earn a profit from a model that already works, and to grow at a pace its own cash allows.

A **startup** is built to find a model that can grow very fast, usually spending outside money long before profits arrive. Paul Graham put it simply: "A startup is a company designed to grow fast." Steve Blank describes it as a temporary search for a business model that can repeat and scale.
Neither size, age nor technology decides which one you are. The design does.

image.label: Two paths: a steady staircase and a steep rocket line
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 완만하게 올라가는 계단("Small business: profit first, steady growth"), 오른쪽은 처음에 아래로 꺼졌다가 가파르게 솟는 J자 곡선("Startup: losses first, fast growth"). 두 길의 출발점은 같은 "$1M".

cards.title: Who pays for growth sets the rules.
body: A small business grows on money from customers and loans. Customers pay only for what they get today, and banks want steady repayment. So profit and cash come first.

A startup often grows on venture money. Those investors expect most of their bets to fail and a few to pay for all the rest. So each bet must have a real chance at a huge outcome. Once you take that money, slow and profitable is no longer good enough.

cards.title: A software company can be a small business.
body: Two developers sell a billing tool to dental offices. No investors, healthy profit, steady growth. That's a **small business** that happens to be software.
A team building a new kind of warehouse robot raises outside money, loses millions, and aims to sell worldwide. That's a startup that happens to be manufacturing.
The choice is about the path, not the product.

cards.title: "Startup" is not a promotion.
body: The startup label can sound more ambitious, so people pick it for status. But the path carries real costs: most attempts fail, you give up ownership, and you answer to investors' timelines.

It's also hard to reverse. Once investors expect fast growth, a steady profitable business can look like a disappointment to them, even if it's a good life for you. Many small businesses grow large over decades without ever taking that trade.

cards.title: Now it's scheduling software.
body: Your booking tool serves 300 physical therapy clinics at $100 a month: $360,000 a year, profitable, growing slowly by word of mouth.
An investor wants to fund you to cover all kinds of health clinics, starting now. What's your move?

options.text: Take the money and build for every clinic type at once
options.feedback: You commit to fast growth before knowing other clinics want your tool. If they don't, you've traded a profitable business for a funded one that's losing money.

options.text: Turn it down and keep growing from profits
options.feedback: Safe and fully yours. But you may be leaving a much bigger opportunity untested.

options.text: Try selling to two other clinic types first, then choose the path
options.feedback: A small test tells you whether fast growth is truly available. Then you pick the path the evidence supports, not the one that sounds bigger.

cards.title: Decide which business you're building before you judge its numbers.
body: A small business wins with profit and steady growth. A startup wins with very fast growth, paid for up front. The same numbers read differently on each path.
**Try it today:** write one line: "My business is built to ___." Then check whether your funding, goals and last year's numbers all match that line.
